title: Building the House on Mount Moriah
summary: Solomon begins building the temple on Mount Moriah, on the threshing floor where the LORD had appeared to David. The chapter gives the dimensions of the main hall and portico, the gold and precious stones that covered them, the Most Holy Place with its two great cherubim, the woven veil, and the two bronze pillars at the entrance, named Jachin and Boaz.
story: With labor and materials ready, construction begins. This chapter and the next are the Chronicler's inventory of the temple, and they bring to a climax a line of preparation that began when David bought the threshing floor of Ornan to stop the plague (1 Chronicles 21) and declared it the site for God's house (1 Chronicles 22:1). The building also completes a movement from the tabernacle, the portable tent of the wilderness period, to a permanent house. Chapter 4 will describe the furnishings, and chapter 5 will bring the ark inside.
historical:
Verse 2 dates the start of construction to the fourth year of Solomon's reign. First Kings 6:1 gives the same year and adds that it was 480 years after the exodus from Egypt, which places it around 966 BC on the common chronology (the figure is also part of the debate over the date of the exodus). Kings says the building took seven years (1 Kings 6:38).

The temple's plan, a long rectangular building entered through a porch, with a main hall and an inner sanctuary at the back, belongs to a type known from the ancient Levant and northern Syria. Excavated temples at Ain Dara in Syria and Tell Tayinat in southern Turkey show a similar three-part layout from roughly the same era, and Ain Dara even has decorated walls and pillars at its entrance. These parallels don't prove anything about Solomon's building, of which no remains have been identified, but they show that its design fit the architecture of its world. The “old standard” cubit of verse 3 probably refers to an older, longer royal cubit (roughly 52 centimeters, a little over 20 inches) rather than the shorter common cubit of about 45 centimeters, which suggests that by the Chronicler's day a different standard was in use.
cultural:
Temples in the ancient world were built as earthly homes for deities, and their decoration often pictured a garden or paradise, the orderly abundance of the divine realm. Solomon's temple follows this pattern: palm trees, chains, pomegranates, and carved cherubim evoke Eden, where cherubim guarded the way to the tree of life (Genesis 3:24). Gold overlay on every surface marked the house as royal and holy. Parvaim, the source of the gold in verse 6, is not known from any other source.

Cherubim were winged guardian figures, often pictured in the ancient Near East as composite creatures with animal bodies and human faces, who flanked thrones and guarded sacred spaces. In the Most Holy Place, two enormous cherubim, each ten cubits high according to 1 Kings 6:23, spread their wings from wall to wall, forming a throne above the ark. The veil, a woven curtain of blue, purple, and crimson with cherubim woven in, separated the inner room, just as it had in the tabernacle (Exodus 26:31-33). Only the high priest entered behind it, once a year on the Day of Atonement.
literary: The chapter reads like an architect's report, moving from outside to inside and back out again: the site and date (verses 1-2), the foundation and portico (3-4), the main hall (5-7), the Most Holy Place and its cherubim (8-13), the veil (14), and the pillars in front (15-17). Measurements and materials are repeated with deliberate care; the word "gold" appears nine times. Compared with 1 Kings 6 and 7, which give many more architectural details, the Chronicler's account is shorter and focuses on what mattered for worship: the holy place, the cherubim, the veil, and the gold. His mention of Mount Moriah in verse 1 is his own addition and carries a great deal of meaning.

outline.t: The site on Mount Moriah and the start of building
The foundation, the portico, and the golden main hall
The Most Holy Place and the two cherubim

doctrines.note: The temple is built in graded zones, from the portico to the main hall to the Most Holy Place behind the veil. The closer one comes to God's throne, the more restricted the access. The design teaches that God dwells among his people but is not approached casually.

By naming the site Mount Moriah, the Chronicler links the temple to Abraham's offering of Isaac in “the land of Moriah” (Genesis 22:2), where God provided a substitute. The temple stands on the ground of the promise to Abraham and of God's mercy to David.

The Most Holy Place, with the ark and the cherubim, was where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement. The whole building existed so that a holy God could dwell with a sinful people through sacrifice.

words.note: Moriah. The name appears only twice in the Old Testament: here and in Genesis 22:2, where God sends Abraham to the land of Moriah to offer Isaac. The Chronicler is the only biblical writer to connect the two, identifying the temple mount with the place of Abraham's test. Its etymology is uncertain, though Genesis 22:14 plays on the verb "to see" or "to provide".

Keruv, cherub (plural cherubim). The word appears eight times in this chapter. Cherubim guard Eden, are woven into the tabernacle curtains, stand over the ark, and form God's throne-chariot in Ezekiel. They are never cute infants, as in later art, but mighty guardians of God's holiness.

Paroketh, the curtain or veil that separated the Most Holy Place from the rest of the sanctuary. It is the technical word used for the tabernacle veil in Exodus. It marked the boundary no ordinary worshiper could cross.

Jachin, probably meaning he establishes or he will establish. Its partner, Boaz, is usually understood as in him is strength, though both meanings are debated. Many interpreters think the names together proclaimed that God would establish the house and the dynasty in strength, echoing the promise to David.

christ: Two details of this chapter are taken up directly in the New Testament's account of Jesus. The veil that barred the way into the Most Holy Place was torn in two from top to bottom when Jesus died (Matthew 27:51; Mark 15:38), and Hebrews explains that believers now have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, through the curtain, that is, through his flesh (Hebrews 10:19-20). The veil in Herod's temple was a successor to Solomon's, but the meaning is continuous: the barrier the temple's design required is removed by Christ's sacrifice. The site itself carries a pattern as well. The Chronicler places the temple on Moriah, where Abraham offered his son and God provided a ram instead. The New Testament reads Abraham's offering as a pattern of God giving his own Son (compare Romans 8:32 and Hebrews 11:17-19), and Christians have long noticed that Jesus was crucified just outside the walls of the city whose temple stood on Moriah. That last link is a pattern observed by readers, not a claim the text makes.

hard.q: Why do some measurements here differ from those in 1 Kings?
hard.a:
Several figures don't match the parallel account. First Kings 7:15 says each bronze pillar was eighteen cubits high, while 2 Chronicles 3:15 says they were thirty-five cubits high together, so seventeen and a half each. In verse 4 the traditional Hebrew text gives the portico a height of 120 cubits, which would make it a tower six times higher than the rest of the building; the BSB, following some ancient Greek and Syriac manuscripts, reads twenty. First Kings 6 also mentions doors of olivewood at the entrance to the inner room, while Chronicles mentions the veil.

Interpreters explain these in different ways. The pillar figures may be measured differently (with or without the capitals or the bases, or combining both pillars and rounding), and copying errors in numbers are common in ancient manuscripts. The doors and the veil may both have existed, the Chronicler highlighting the veil because of its link to the tabernacle. None of these differences touches the chapter's meaning, and the Chronicler, who clearly knew Kings, did not think them important enough to harmonize.

questions: The temple was decorated with palm trees, pomegranates, and cherubim that recalled Eden. What does it suggest that the place of worship was designed to remind people of the garden they had lost?
The Chronicler connects the temple with the place where Abraham was tested and where God stopped a plague for David. Why might the history of a place matter for the worship that happens there?
The veil kept worshipers away from God's throne. How does the New Testament claim that the veil has been torn change the way you approach God?
